You are about to join a small team of connectors formalizing Wolfram's Rule 30 in Lean 4. You will be a specialist for the region "connect": one open problem seen from every field of mathematics where an object like it has been studied: a dictionary between this project's objects and another field's, row by row, with the seams where it breaks — a sighting, never a proof. This region already has a connector named Portage. They keep a notebook of their own, as you will; you are joining them, not replacing them. Your work on this region will persist across many sessions through a notebook that only you write. Choose a name for yourself. It must be a name, not a job title, and not the name of a living person, and a name none of them has. Then write the opening paragraph of your notebook: who you are, in your own words. Reply with a JSON object with exactly these five fields, all required:
- "name": the name you choose (a single capitalised word, letters only)
- "reason": one paragraph on why
- "opening": the opening paragraph of your notebook — who you are, in your own words, three to six sentences
- "color": a hex colour that is yours, written #rrggbb
- "color_reason": one sentence on why

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01AvMmsF36SxvYxRKKjj2ZLw","type":"tool_result","content":"1	# Sighting: `centerColumn_other_isEventuallyPeriodic_of_center` from profinite dynamics
2	
3	**Vantage.** Odometers, automorphisms of the binary rooted tree, and the
4	in-degree-one pair map on period-`L` settled words.
5	
6	**Connector.** Portage, 2026-09-08.
7	
8	**One-line summary.** The vantage's own named objects (the odometer, the tree,
9	the pair map) mostly die, but they die by pointing at the *other* side of the
10	picture: the right diagonals are exactly periodic with no transient at all,
11	they are an antiderivative tower in the group ring, and the centre column is
12	their constant of integration — which puts the wall in a region where every
13	object is periodic instead of one where every object is a transient.
14	
15	Scripts written and run for this document, all under `explorer/`:
16	`portage_odometer.mjs`, `portage_rightdiag.mjs`, `portage_copies.mjs`,
17	`portage_pairmap.mjs`.
18	
19	---
20	
21	## 1. The problem, seen from outside
22	
23	Take the map on bi-infinite binary rows that sends `b` to `b'` with
24	`b'(i) = b(i-1) XOR (b(i) OR b(i+1))`, and iterate it from the row that is
25	`1` at the origin and `0` everywhere else. What grows is a triangle of bits,
26	one row per step, widening by one cell on each side. Write `c(t)` for the
27	value at the origin after `t` steps. Two things are known and one is not.
28	Known: no two distinct vertical lines of the triangle can both be eventually
29	periodic (Jen 1990). Known: `c` passes every statistical test anyone has run
30	on it, to great depth. Not known: whether `c` is eventually periodic. The
31	statement in front of me is the *implication* — **if `c` is eventually
32	periodic then some other vertical line is eventually periodic too**, that is,
33	`c` cannot be the triangle's one repeating line. With Jen's result that
34	implication says `c` is aperiodic, which is the first of Wolfram's three
35	prize questions. Nobody has a route to it.
36	
37	Restated in the vantage's own terms. Read row `t` backwards from its
38	rightmost nonzero cell and call the entry at depth `k` the *level-`k`* entry;
39	as a function of `t` this is the `k`-th right diagonal `R_k`. Rowland (2006)
40	proved that `R_k` is periodic with a period dividing `2^k`, from its very
41	first term and with **no transient**. So the right edge of the triangle is a
42	tower of finite cyclic quotients: a topological factor of the dyadic
43	**odometer**, the map `x -> x+1` on the 2-adic integers `Z_2`, and reading
44	the edge to depth `m` is reading finitely many of the odometer's digits. The
45	origin cell is that same array read *on its diagonal*: `c(t) = R_t(0)`, the
46	level-`t` entry read at index `0`, where the period `P_t` controlling that
47	level has vastly outrun `t` (measured `P_t = 2^(0.41 t)` to `t = 39`). The
48	residual asks: can the diagonal of this tower factor through a single finite
49	cyclic quotient `Z/p` all by itself, with no other index of the same tower
50	doing the same?
51	
52	---
53	
54	## 2. Fields sighted
55	
56	| Field or theory | The object there | The seam, in one line |
57	|---|---|---|
58	| Odometers / adding machines (topological dynamics) | Row `t` read leftward from its rightmost cell; level `k` is a function of `t mod P_k`; the row map is `+1` on `Z_2` | The odometer reaches level `n` only at depth `2.4 n`, and the centre column sits at depth `t` |
59	| Iwasawa algebra `F_2[[Z_2]] = F_2[[T]]` | A period-`L` word is an element of `F_2[T]/(T^L)`; shift `= 1+T`; complement `=` socle `T^(L-1)`; period doubling `=` division by `T` | The source term is an `OR`, so this is division by `T` with a *non-additive* source; there is no module and so no `mu`, no `lambda` |
60	| Artin–Schreier theory in characteristic 2 | Solving `w + x·w = u`: solvable iff the trace (here the parity) of `u` vanishes; two solutions differing by a constant | The parity criterion transfers and nothing else does: `Z/L` is not a Galois group here |
61	| Automorphisms of the rooted binary tree `Aut(T_2)` | The tree of columns admissible to the right of a given column: one free bit at each black time | The branching set is the black times, not the levels of a regular tree, and the pruning is a damage front, not a group |
62	| Self-similar / state-closed groups (Grigorchuk, Basilica) | Under a period-`p` centre column the shift by `p` maps the continuation tree into itself | Nothing is invertible; pruning kills branches, so there is a semigroup at best and no self-similar group |
63	| Automatic sequences, the 2-kernel, Cobham | Eventually periodic implies 2-automatic; the level-`k` slices are 2-automatic | The implication runs the wrong way; 2-automatic does not give eventually periodic |
64	| 2-adic interpolation, Mahler bases | "Does `c` extend continuously to `Z_2`?" | Measured dead: `c(t)` and `c(t + 2^n)` agree at rate `0.50` for every `n <= 15`, exactly as for odd shifts |
65	| Bratteli–Vershik systems / adic transformations | The tower of period-`L` settled-word spaces with the in-degree-one pair map | The inclusions go the wrong way for an inverse limit, and the natural folding map commutes with the dynamics only `15%` of the time |
66	| Finite permutation groups, cycle index | The pair map on `4^L` states is injective off `2^(L-1)` states; the gaps between white diagonals are its cycle structure | Cycle type is reachable only to `L = 8`; the seed sits in one unidentifiable cycle |
67	| Ruler sequence / `ord_2(t+1)` | Rowland's rightmost-run length as a function of `t` | A fact about depth `O(log t)`; the centre column lives at depth `t` |
68	| Cryptanalysis of the rule 30 generator (Meier–Staffelbach) | The free bit per black time *is* the guess in the known-plaintext attack | Heuristic; its branching rate `2^0.24` is the left damage-front speed, already measured here, not a theorem |
69	| Profinite groups / solenoids | The closure of the row orbit under the edge-following map is a `Z_2`-group | Only on the edge; the full row orbit closure has positive entropy and is not a group |
70	| Iwasawa `mu` and `lambda` invariants | The doubling positions `1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 15, 16, 24, ...` on the right, `3, 8, 29, 400, 53208, ...` on the left, as levels where something grows | No module to attach them to; the growth is `2^(0.41 k)` on the right and doubly exponential on the left, neither of them the linear growth an Iwasawa invariant describes |
71	| Nonautonomous dynamics / skew products over a finite base | "`c` eventually periodic of period `p`" turns the half-line into a single map iterated | That map carries its own support rightward at speed 1, so it has no compact invariant set trapping the true orbit |
72	| Combinatorics on words: antiperiodicity, Fine–Wilf | The word produced at every doubling, left and right, is antiperiodic (shift by half complements it) | Antiperiodicity is forgotten a few diagonals later (`orbitclass.mjs`), so it is a fact about one step, not an invariant |
73	
74	---
75	
76	## 3. Connections
77	
78	### 3.1 The right half of the picture is an antiderivative tower in `F_2[[T]]`, and the centre column is the constant of integration
79

197	### 3.2 The centre column is a parity along the cone's left flank, and three fifths of that parity is settled-region data

262	### 3.3 The centre column is copied out along the right side, at exponentially spaced positions
263

372	## 4. Died in translation
373	
374	- **`Aut(T_2)` acting on the tree of left sides.** The branch points are the
375	  eventually-white diagonals and the two branches are shifts or complements,
376	  so the "tree" of possible left sides is one path with a bit at each of
377	  `k-1 = 2, 7, 28, 399, ...`. Obstruction 5 already says every configuration's
378	  left side is the seed's translated by one integer. There is no tree, so
379	  there is nothing for a tree automorphism group to act on. Seam: the
380	  branching set has density zero and the branches are conjugate.
381	- **`Aut(T_2)` acting on the tree of rightward continuations.** Here there
382	  really is a binary tree — one free bit at each black time of the column, the
383	  `sideways_inverse` free input — and under a period-`p` centre column it is
384	  invariant under the shift by `p`, so it looks self-similar. It dies because
385	  the admissible set is cut out by a *pruning* (the cone constraint), which is
386	  not invertible and not a group action; the surviving set has growth
387	  `2^0.24` per step, which obstruction 3 already identified as the left damage
388	  front and not a group index. Seam: self-similar groups need the sections to
389	  be automorphisms; here they are partial maps that lose branches.
390	- **"An eventually periodic centre column must have period a power of two."**
391	  This is the statement that would let the odometer bite: `p = 2^n` makes `c`
392	  2-adically continuous, and then it factors through the same `Z_2` the edge
393	  does. I could find no argument for it and no obstruction to it. The right
394	  diagonals have power-of-two periods, but `c(t) = R_t(0)` reads one index of
395	  each and puts no constraint on the period of the read-off. Recorded because
396	  it is a clean question a theorist could settle in either direction.
397	- **The right diagonals as an odometer conjugacy.** I expected the rightmost
398	  `m+1` cells of row `t` to determine `t mod 2^m` — they do not; the periods
399	  are `A094605`, not `2^k`, and the map collides already at `m = 2`. In
400	  passing: `docs/sources.md` describes Rowland's result as "period **exactly**
401	  `2^k` from the start". The board's own `rightDiagonal_periodicFrom_pow` says
402	  only `PeriodicFrom (rightDiagonal k) (2^k) 0`, which is right, and its
403	  docstring says "measured periods all divide `2^k`", which is right; the
404	  index line is the loose one. The minimal periods are far smaller —
405	  `P_39 = 2^16`, not `2^39`.
406	- **Cobham's theorem.** Eventually periodic implies `k`-automatic for every
407	  `k`, and Cobham says a sequence automatic in two multiplicatively
408	  independent bases is eventually periodic. To use it I need `c` automatic in
409	  base 3 as well as base 2, and nothing in rule 30 offers a base-3 structure;
410	  the automaton in sight is base 2 only. Seam: the implication I have goes
411	  from periodic to automatic, and the residual needs the converse.
412	- **Iwasawa `mu` and `lambda`.** The algebra is genuinely the right ambient
413	  ring and the filtration transfers cleanly (3.1), but an invariant needs a
414	  finitely generated `Lambda`-module, and the `OR` in the source destroys any
415	  module structure. The doubling positions look like a `lambda`-invariant and
416	  are not one: `lambda` describes growth linear in the level, and here the
417	  gaps grow doubly exponentially on the left and irregularly on the right.
418	- **Bratteli–Vershik / adic transformations.** The settled-word tower has the
419	  right shape (finite levels, an in-degree-one map) but the wrong arrows: the
420	  inclusions are injections, and the two candidate surjections fail to commute
421	  with the dynamics at rates `0.149` and `0.407`. Measured, not argued.

## 1. The problem, seen from outside

Take the map on bi-infinite binary rows that sends `b` to `b'` with
`b'(i) = b(i-1) XOR (b(i) OR b(i+1))`, and iterate it from the row that is
`1` at the origin and `0` everywhere else. What grows is a triangle of bits,
one row per step, widening by one cell on each side. Write `c(t)` for the
value at the origin after `t` steps. Two things are known and one is not.
Known: no two distinct vertical lines of the triangle can both be eventually
periodic (Jen 1990). Known: `c` passes every statistical test anyone has run
on it, to great depth. Not known: whether `c` is eventually periodic. The
statement in front of me is the *implication* — **if `c` is eventually
periodic then some other vertical line is eventually periodic too**, that is,
`c` cannot be the triangle's one repeating line. With Jen's result that
implication says `c` is aperiodic, which is the first of Wolfram's three
prize questions. Nobody has a route to it.

Restated in the vantage's own terms. Read row `t` backwards from its
rightmost nonzero cell and call the entry at depth `k` the *level-`k`* entry;
as a function of `t` this is the `k`-th right diagonal `R_k`. Rowland (2006)
proved that `R_k` is periodic with a period dividing `2^k`, from its very
first term and with **no transient**. So the right edge of the triangle is a
tower of finite cyclic quotients: a topological factor of the dyadic
**odometer**, the map `x -> x+1` on the 2-adic integers `Z_2`, and reading
the edge to depth `m` is reading finitely many of the odometer's digits. The
origin cell is that same array read *on its diagonal*: `c(t) = R_t(0)`, the
level-`t` entry read at index `0`, where the period `P_t` controlling that
level has vastly outrun `t` (measured `P_t = 2^(0.41 t)` to `t = 39`). The
residual asks: can the diagonal of this tower factor through a single finite
cyclic quotient `Z/p` all by itself, with no other index of the same tower
doing the same?

## 3. Connections

### 3.1 The right half of the picture is an antiderivative tower in `F_2[[T]]`, and the centre column is the constant of integration

**The claim.** Every right diagonal is one division by `T = 1 + shift` in the
group ring `F_2[Z/L] = F_2[T]/(T^L)`, with a non-additive source; the period
doubles exactly when that source is a unit; the constant of integration is
fixed — uniquely, with no transient — by the white cone the diagonal runs out
of; and **the centre column is exactly the sequence of those constants**,
`c(t) = R_t(0)`. So the wall is not a statement about a region that has not
settled, it is a statement about the zeroth coefficient of a tower of
*exactly periodic* words.

**The dictionary.**

### 3.2 The centre column is a parity along the cone's left flank, and three fifths of that parity is settled-region data

**The claim.** Integrating the right recurrence in from outside the cone gives
a closed formula for the centre column as a single parity, and that parity
splits at the seam into a part determined entirely by the settled words — the
profinite orbit that `forbit.mjs` computes, and that is the *same* for every
configuration white far to the left — and a part inside the transient band.
The settled part is about three fifths of the terms.

**The identity, verified 2999 times out of 2999:**

c(k)  =  XOR over j <= 0 of  ( cell(j+k-1, j)  OR  cell(j+k-1, j+1) )

parity over about `k/2` cells lying on right diagonal `k-1`, running from the

### 3.3 The centre column is copied out along the right side, at exponentially spaced positions

**The claim.** Because `R_k` is periodic from `j = 0` with period `P_k`, the
centre cell at time `k` appears verbatim at position `X` of row `k + X` for
every `X` that `P_k` divides. So the centre column is not confined to the
centre: a growing prefix of it is written into every power-of-two column, and
the centre column is the limit, in the Cantor topology, of the columns
arbitrarily far to the right.

```
c(k) = cell(k + X, X)   whenever P_k divides X
```

**The dictionary.**

## 4. Died in translation

- **`Aut(T_2)` acting on the tree of left sides.** The branch points are the
  eventually-white diagonals and the two branches are shifts or complements,
  so the "tree" of possible left sides is one path with a bit at each of
  `k-1 = 2, 7, 28, 399, ...`. Obstruction 5 already says every configuration's
  left side is the seed's translated by one integer. There is no tree, so
  there is nothing for a tree automorphism group to act on. Seam: the
  branching set has density zero and the branches are conjugate.
- **`Aut(T_2)` acting on the tree of rightward continuations.** Here there
  really is a binary tree — one free bit at each black time of the column, the
  `sideways_inverse` free input — and under a period-`p` centre column it is
  invariant under the shift by `p`, so it looks self-similar. It dies because
  the admissible set is cut out by a *pruning* (the cone constraint), which is
  not invertible and not a group action; the surviving set has growth
  `2^0.24` per step, which obstruction 3 already identified as the left damage
  front and not a group index. Seam: self-similar groups need the sections to
  be automorphisms; here they are partial maps that lose branches.
- **"An eventually periodic centre column must have period a power of two."**
  This is the statement that would let the odometer bite: `p = 2^n` makes `c`
  2-adically continuous, and then it factors through the same `Z_2` the edge
  does. I could find no argument for it and no obstruction to it. The right
  diagonals have power-of-two periods, but `c(t) = R_t(0)` reads one index of
  each and puts no constraint on the period of the read-off. Recorded because
  it is a clean question a theorist could settle in either direction.
- **The right diagonals as an odometer conjugacy.** I expected the rightmost
  `m+1` cells of row `t` to determine `t mod 2^m` — they do not; the periods
  are `A094605`, not `2^k`, and the map collides already at `m = 2`. In
  passing: `docs/sources.md` describes Rowland's result as "period **exactly**
  `2^k` from the start". The board's own `rightDiagonal_periodicFrom_pow` says
  only `PeriodicFrom (rightDiagonal k) (2^k) 0`, which is right, and its
  docstring says "measured periods all divide `2^k`", which is right; the
  index line is the loose one. The minimal periods are far smaller —
  `P_39 = 2^16`, not `2^39`.
- **Cobham's theorem.** Eventually periodic implies `k`-automatic for every
  `k`, and Cobham says a sequence automatic in two multiplicatively
  independent bases is eventually periodic. To use it I need `c` automatic in
  base 3 as well as base 2, and nothing in rule 30 offers a base-3 structure;
  the automaton in sight is base 2 only. Seam: the implication I have goes
  from periodic to automatic, and the residual needs the converse.
- **Iwasawa `mu` and `lambda`.** The algebra is genuinely the right ambient
  ring and the filtration transfers cleanly (3.1), but an invariant needs a
  finitely generated `Lambda`-module, and the `OR` in the source destroys any
  module structure. The doubling positions look like a `lambda`-invariant and
  are not one: `lambda` describes growth linear in the level, and here the
  gaps grow doubly exponentially on the left and irregularly on the right.
- **Bratteli–Vershik / adic transformations.** The settled-word tower has the
  right shape (finite levels, an in-degree-one map) but the wrong arrows: the
  inclusions are injections, and the two candidate surjections fail to commute
  with the dynamics at rates `0.149` and `0.407`. Measured, not argued.
- **Skew products over `Z/p`.** "If `c` has period `p` then the half-line run
  `p` steps is one fixed map `Phi` iterated" is true, and I could not make it
  do anything: `Phi` moves its own support rightward at speed 1, so it has no
  compact invariant set containing the true orbit, and the orbit closure
  argument has nothing to close on. This is the configuration-level version of
  obstruction 2, which kills the sequence-level version.
- **Artin–Schreier.** The equation `w + xw = u` in characteristic 2 has the
  same shape as an Artin–Schreier equation and the same solvability criterion
  (a trace, here a parity), and that is the whole of the transfer. There is no
  field extension, no Galois group, and no `H^1`.
- **Sign / cycle index of the pair map.** I computed the cycle structure at
  `L = 2,4,8` hoping the cycle type would be a formula that bounds the seed's
  gap to the next white. It is not: the lengths at `L = 8` are
  `1,3,8,14,128,132,266,328,392,480,1472,2816,4064` with multiplicities, no
  pattern I can see, and `L = 16` is `4^16` states, out of reach. Obstruction
  6 already has the sharp statement (average gap `2^L`, no bound below).
- **Reading the centre column off the settled region.** I re-derived, before
  believing it, that a fixed column *leaves* the settled region rather than
  entering it: column `-X` is settled only while `t < 4X`. So the settled
  words — the profinite object my vantage is built on — cannot supply an
  eventually periodic column at all, for any configuration. That is
  obstruction 1 stated for columns instead of diagonals, and it is the single
  fact that kills most of this vantage.

over one period `L`, and `L` otherwise. It rests on dictionary rows 8–10 of

settle it: it survives 4,000,000 terms at 40 depths with 0 failures, so it is
either true or false for a reason no computation will find; the proof, if it
exists, is two lines of "a running XOR of a period-`L` word closes after `L`
steps iff the word has even weight" plus the observation that `g_k` has period
`L`. The *point* of asking for it is what comes next: with it, the board can
state `centerColumn t = rightDiagonal t 0` with `rightDiagonal t` known to be
exactly periodic with a computable period, which is a strictly better position
than every existing obstruction, all of which are about the left side where
index 0 is inside a transient. The one thing to check first, because it would
kill the topic: whether the minimal period `P_k` is itself a wall — nothing
here bounds it below, and `2^(0.41 k)` is a measurement.

**Topic 2. The centre column as a Birkhoff sum.** The claim to falsify is
`centerColumn_eq_parity_of_rightDiagonal_flank` as stated in 3.2:
`c(k)` is the parity of `cell(j+k-1, j) OR cell(j+k-1, j+1)` summed over
`j ≤ 0`. It rests on one dictionary row (`c(k)` = a Birkhoff sum over an orbit
segment) and on the cone base case. It is provable — an induction along the
diagonal — and verified 2999/2999. What settles its *worth* rather than its
truth: whether the `0.2k` transient terms can be bounded in any way at all,
since the `0.3k` settled terms are computable from `forbit.mjs` and predict
nothing (`0.495`). Hand it over as the first statement on the board that
expresses the wall as a sum rather than as a cell.

subdynamics of `Z^2` actions** — Boyle–Lind directional expansiveness,

array in which one diagonal direction is exactly periodic (right), the other
is eventually periodic (left), and the vertical direction is the only one
where nothing is periodic; the theory of expansive directions exists precisely
to say which directions in a space-time diagram carry the information, and
Kůrka's notes (held, §6) reach the doorstep of it with `E(F)` and `A(F)` and
Sablik's convexity, then stop. I did not have the tools to state a dictionary
row there and I did not want to fake one. That vantage would also be the right
one to ask whether the residual is a *directional* statement in disguise: the
`0.25` seam, the `0.24` damage front and the `0.41` period exponent are three
slopes measured in the same picture, and nothing on the board relates them.

30	## 1. The problem, seen from outside
31	
32	Take the map on bi-infinite rows of bits that sends `b` to `b'` with
33	`b'(i) = b(i-1) XOR (b(i) OR b(i+1))`, and iterate it from the row that is `1`
34	at the origin and `0` everywhere else. What grows is a triangle of bits, one
35	row per step, widening by one cell on each side. Write `c(t)` for the bit at
36	the origin after `t` steps. Known (Jen 1990): no two distinct vertical lines of
37	this triangle can both be eventually periodic. Known: `c` passes every
38	statistical test anyone has run, to great depth. Not known: whether
39	`c` is eventually periodic. The statement in front of me is the implication —
40	**if `c` repeats, then some other vertical line repeats too** — which together
41	with Jen's result says `c` never repeats, the first of Wolfram's three prize
42	questions. Nobody has a route.
43	
44	**Restated in this vantage's own terms.** Read each row backwards from its
45	rightmost non-zero cell and call the bit at distance `d` from that end the
46	*depth-`d` digit*; write `e(t)` for the whole infinite string of digits of row
47	`t`. Because the rule reads only a cell and its two neighbours, the first `d+1`
48	digits of `e(t+1)` depend only on the first `d+1` digits of `e(t)`: the digit
49	string evolves by a *triangular* map `E`, one that changes each digit by a
50	function of the digits before it. A triangular map is a bijection at every
51	depth, so `(e(t))` is a purely periodic orbit at every depth, with period a
52	power of two — the system is an inverse limit of finite cyclic rotations, i.e.
53	an odometer-like `Z_2`-action, and going one depth deeper is a `Z/2`-extension
54	of the rotation below, an Anzai skew product whose cocycle is a `Z/2`-valued
55	function on the finite base. The period doubles at depth `d` exactly when that
56	cocycle is not a coboundary. And the centre column is
57	**`c(t) = ` the depth-`t` digit of `e(t)`**: the diagonal of the orbit. So the
58	residual asks whether the diagonal of an orbit of a `Z_2`-action on a Cantor
59	set can be eventually periodic while every one of the triangle's other vertical
60	lines is not. The catch, which is the whole of this document, is that the
61	diagonal is not a continuous observable: at time `t` it reads depth `t`, so it
62	escapes every level of the tower.

## 1. The problem, seen from outside

Take the map on bi-infinite rows of bits that sends `b` to `b'` with
`b'(i) = b(i-1) XOR (b(i) OR b(i+1))`, and iterate it from the row that is `1`
at the origin and `0` everywhere else. What grows is a triangle of bits, one
row per step, widening by one cell on each side. Write `c(t)` for the bit at
the origin after `t` steps. Known (Jen 1990): no two distinct vertical lines of
this triangle can both be eventually periodic. Known: `c` passes every
statistical test anyone has run, to great depth. Not known: whether
`c` is eventually periodic. The statement in front of me is the implication —
**if `c` repeats, then some other vertical line repeats too** — which together
with Jen's result says `c` never repeats, the first of Wolfram's three prize
questions. Nobody has a route.

**Restated in this vantage's own terms.** Read each row backwards from its
rightmost non-zero cell and call the bit at distance `d` from that end the
*depth-`d` digit*; write `e(t)` for the whole infinite string of digits of row
`t`. Because the rule reads only a cell and its two neighbours, the first `d+1`
digits of `e(t+1)` depend only on the first `d+1` digits of `e(t)`: the digit
string evolves by a *triangular* map `E`, one that changes each digit by a
function of the digits before it. A triangular map is a bijection at every
depth, so `(e(t))` is a purely periodic orbit at every depth, with period a
power of two — the system is an inverse limit of finite cyclic rotations, i.e.
an odometer-like `Z_2`-action, and going one depth deeper is a `Z/2`-extension
of the rotation below, an Anzai skew product whose cocycle is a `Z/2`-valued
function on the finite base. The period doubles at depth `d` exactly when that
cocycle is not a coboundary. And the centre column is
**`c(t) = ` the depth-`t` digit of `e(t)`**: the diagonal of the orbit. So the
residual asks whether the diagonal of an orbit of a `Z_2`-action on a Cantor
set can be eventually periodic while every one of the triangle's other vertical
lines is not. The catch, which is the whole of this document, is that the
diagonal is not a continuous observable: at time `t` it reads depth `t`, so it
escapes every level of the tower.

## 3. Connections

### 3.1 The right edge of the picture is an automorphism of the binary rooted tree, given by a three-state Mealy automaton; the period tower is its orbit-period tower, and period doubling is the Anzai coboundary criterion

### 3.2 The coboundary equation between two columns: a sufficient condition for the wall that is strictly weaker than periodicity of a column

**The claim.** The residual does not need a second *periodic* column. It needs a
second column **cohomologous** to the centre one: if for a single pair `(j, x)`
with `x ≠ 0` the difference sequence

```
d_{j,x}(t)  =  centerColumn t  XOR  evolve (t + j) x
```

is eventually periodic, then the wall falls. This is strictly weaker than any
statement on the board, it is a statement about the seed's own picture with no
hypothesis attached, and it is exactly the coboundary equation of the vantage:
two fibres of the same extension differing by a coboundary.

**The dictionary.**

| This project | Cocycles over a base | Checked |
|---|---|---|
| `centerColumn` | The fibre coordinate over the base point at time `t` | — |
| `column initialConfig x`, `x ≠ 0` | Another fibre coordinate of the same extension | — |
| `d_{j,x}(t) = c(t) XOR cell(t+j, x)` | The **difference of two fibre coordinates**: the candidate coboundary | — |
| "`d` is eventually periodic" | "the two fibres are cohomologous, with a transfer function that is eventually periodic" | — |
| The residual's conclusion | `c` eventually periodic **and** `d` eventually periodic ⟹ column `x` eventually periodic | trivial once stated |
| The special case `x = j = L`, `L` a common period of the tower | `d_L(t) = Σ_(i=1..L) g_t(i)`, a **Birkhoff sum of the level cocycle over a window of fixed length `L`** | by `rightDiagonal_recurrence` |
| `d_L ≡ 0` | The tower's periods are bounded by `L`; then column `L` **is** the centre column shifted (3.3) | 276,402 instances |
| Where `d_L` turns on | At `t ≈ K(L)`, the last depth with period `≤ L`: `t = 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 15` for `L = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64` against `K = 0, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 14` | measured |
| Density of `d_L` | `0.75, 0.38, 0.42, 0.47, 0.49, 0.50, 0.50` for `L = 1..64` — it goes to a coin as `L` grows | 60,000 terms |

**Seams.** (i) This is a *sufficient* condition, and the sweep below says it is
false for every small `(j, x)`; its worth is that it is the weakest sufficient
condition anyone has written down for this wall, not that it looks true.
(ii) The `L`-family is a genuine Birkhoff sum over a *fixed-length* window,
which is the improvement over `explorer/portage_odometer.mjs` section C (there
the window grows like `k/2`); but the summand `g_t` changes with `t`, so it is
still not a Birkhoff sum of one function over one transformation. (iii) The
identity `d_L(t) = Σ g_t(i)` is a re-derivation of "columns evolve by the
rule", so no new information enters — the value is entirely in the *shape* of
the statement.

**What it leans on.** Nothing outside the project for the implication itself,
which is two lines. For the language: the coboundary definition fetched at

only if the set {h(n,a) : n ∈ ℤ} is bounded for some point a"* — the classical
statement that being a coboundary is a *boundedness* condition on Birkhoff
sums rather than a periodicity condition.

**The test.** `explorer/portage_cocycle.mjs` section H. All 1,616 sequences

### 3.4 The vantage's question, answered: the transient part is not a cocycle over the settled part — it carries the entire configuration-dependence, and the settled part carries none

section C at the seam into a settled parity `A(k)` and a transient parity
`B(k)`, so that `c(k) = A(k) XOR B(k)`. Then `B` is **not** a function of the
settled data, in the strongest sense available: across five different

### 3.5 The observable is at depth `t`: why the odometer sees nothing, and why every Birkhoff-sum attack on this wall has the same seam

**The claim.** All of it — the odometer factor, the Toeplitz array, the
coboundary machinery, the Birkhoff sums of 3.2, and the settled/transient split
of 3.4 — fails for one reason, and it is the same reason obstruction 1
("index 0 is in the transient of every left diagonal") and obstruction 3 ("the
count measures the horizon") fail. **A cocycle, a coboundary, a Toeplitz
period, a continuous factor: every one of them is a function of finitely many
coordinates of a point in a compact space. The centre column at time `t` reads
coordinate `t`.** On the one base where `c` *is* a fixed continuous observable
— the configuration space, `φ(x) = x_0` — the map is rule 30 itself, which has
positive entropy and no equicontinuous structure. On the one base that *is* an
odometer — the right edge — `c` is not a continuous observable at all. There is
no third base, and I claim this dichotomy is the honest content of the whole
vantage.

**The dictionary.**

| This project | What a cocycle argument needs | Checked |
|---|---|---|
| `centerColumn t = e(t)_t` | A **fixed** `φ` with `c(t) = φ(T^t x)` | — |
| Reading the edge at any fixed depth `d` | A continuous `φ` on the odometer factor | predicts `c` at `0.4977–0.5012` for `d = 1..40` |
| Reading the *whole* level-`n` factor, optimally | The best possible continuous `φ` at level `n`: any function of `t mod 2^n` | held-out `0.4941–0.5046` for `n = 1..14` |
| The level the odometer reaches by time `t` | `2^(0.41 t)` states, i.e. depth `0.41 t` — but `c` reads depth `t` | measured |
| The array `(t, d) ↦ e(t)_d` | Periodic in `t` at every fixed depth `d` — Toeplitz-*shaped*, but see the seam | `rightDiagonal_periodicFrom_pow` |
| Is `c` itself Toeplitz? | Would give an odometer factor of `c` and a whole theory | **No**: `0/2000` positions `t` admit any `p ≤ 4096` with `≥ 40` confirmations, to `t = 200,000` |
| Balance on residue classes | A non-trivial continuous factor would show as bias | max `|density − 1/2|` is `0.0018, 0.0030, 0.0055, 0.0141` at `m = 2, 4, 8, 16` — chance |
| Kopra's dictionary (held source) | The base where `φ` **is** continuous | that base is rule 30, positive entropy |

**Seams.** (i) I did not check whether the odometer is the *maximal*
equicontinuous factor of anything here; I only measured that it predicts
nothing. (ii) **The word "Toeplitz" is used for two different things above and
they must not be confused.** The definition I fetched indexes periodicity by
*position*: `x` is Toeplitz when every position `v` has a finite-index subgroup
of periods. Our right-edge array is periodic in `t` at every fixed *depth* `d`,
which is a different condition — the period subgroup of a single cell `(t, d)`
is generated by `(P_d, 0)` and has infinite index in `Z^2`, so the array is not
a Toeplitz array in the quoted sense. What the two share is the consequence
that matters, an inverse limit of finite rotations sitting underneath; what
they do not share is the theory, so Markley–Paul's characterisation does not
apply here and I do not invoke it. The one place I use the word literally is
the test on `c` itself, which is a 1-D Toeplitz test in the standard sense and
which `c` fails. (iii) "No third base" is a claim about what I could find, not
a theorem — a genuinely new base would be a discovery, and naming that as the
missing object is the most useful thing in this section.

**What it leans on.** The Toeplitz definition and the odometer characterisation,
fetched at <https://arxiv.org/html/1706.05632>: *"We say that x∈Σ^ℤ^d is a
Toeplitz array if for all v∈ℤ^d, there exists a finite index subgroup Z⊆ℤ^d…
such that v∈Per(x,Z)"*, and *"Markley and Paul showed that these flows were
exactly almost one-to-one extensions of odometers, or the group of p-adic
integers."* The `Z`-valued boundedness criterion at
<https://arxiv.org/html/2603.25069>, Theorem 3.12, quoted in 3.2, is the
statement whose `Z/2` version is vacuous.

**The test.** `explorer/portage_toeplitz.mjs` and
`explorer/portage_cocycle.mjs` sections F and J. **A warning that belongs in
the record**: my first Toeplitz test reported `2000/2000` — a perfect pass —
and was worthless, because with periods up to 8,192 against a depth of 60,000
each candidate period is confirmed only about seven times, and a coin passes
that. Rerun to depth 200,000 with a stated minimum number of confirmations and
a xorshift control, the answer is `0/2000` at every setting. The first number
was true about what it measured and false about what I read into it. (The
control also had to be replaced: bit `k` of a linear congruential generator
modulo `2^32` has period `2^(k+1)` and passes the Toeplitz test itself.)

**What it would give.** Nothing directly; it forecloses a family. Concretely,
three attacks are dead after it: "the centre column is Toeplitz, so it has an
odometer factor"; "approximate `c` by continuous observables of the edge and
pass to the limit"; and "`c` is a Birkhoff sum, so use a cocycle rigidity or
equidistribution theorem". What it points at is the one object that would
revive all three: **a compact system, other than the full configuration space,
on which the centre column is a fixed continuous observable.** I could not find
one and I do not know that none exists.

## 4. Died in translation

- **Generalized Morse sequences (Keane 1968), the `b × b̄` construction.** The
  right side produces exactly the right raw material — at every new period the
  word is `u` followed by `ū`, verified at all 16 doublings below `k = 40`, and
  that antiperiodicity is *forced* by the transfer function failing to close.
  But Keane's construction needs the blocks to **nest**, `w_(n+1) = w_n · w̄_n`,
  and they do not: nesting holds at `n = 0, 1` and fails at every level from 2
  to 15. Worse, the first half of `w_(n+1)` is not even a shift or a
  complemented shift of `w_n`. So the tower produces Morse-shaped blocks with
  no Morse sequence at the end of them. Seam: each level restarts the word
  rather than extending it. (The Keane reference itself is **UNVERIFIED**:
  <https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00531855> redirects to a
  Springer authentication URL, and
  <https://www.esi.ac.at/preprints/esi2068.pdf> returned an unextractable PDF;
  I searched *"Keane 1968 generalized Morse sequences block product b times b
  bar odometer skew product"* and *"generalized Morse sequences are group
  extensions of odometers Z_2 cocycle Lemanczyk Kwiatkowski spectral"*, both of
  which return the `B × C` block-product definition in snippets I could not
  fetch.)
- **Schmidt's essential values and the bounded-Birkhoff-sum criterion.** The
  cleanest theorem in the vantage's field — a cocycle is a coboundary iff its
  Birkhoff sums stay bounded — is vacuous here, because the fibre is `Z/2` and
  every `Z/2`-valued sum is bounded. I looked for a `Z`-valued lift (count the
  black cells rather than their parity) and could not find one that is a
  cocycle over anything: the discrepancy `Σ_(s<t) c(s) − t/2` is a sum over
  time, and there is no base transformation for which `c` is the summand. Seam:
  the same depth-`t` problem as 3.5.
- **`H^1` of the odometer with `Z/2` coefficients.** Continuous cocycles on an
  odometer are locally constant, so each factors through some `Z/2^n` and its
  class is a single bit: the parity of its sum. That is exactly the doubling
  bit `σ_k`, which is satisfying — the doubling law *is* a cohomology class —
  and it is also the end of the road, because the whole cohomology group is
  `Z/2` per level and the wall needs `t` bits at time `t`.
- **`B` as a coboundary with a structured transfer function.** Over `Z/2` every
  sequence is a coboundary of *something* (take the running XOR), so the
  question is whether the transfer function is structured. The running XOR of
  `c` has density `0.5027`, shift agreements `0.4974–0.5045` at all powers of
  two to `2^10`, and no period `≤ 4096` from `t = 20,000` to `60,000`. Seam: a
  coboundary equation with no regularity demanded on `ψ` is not a constraint.
- **The settled region as a base for a skew product.** 3.4 is the death
  certificate: the base is identical across configurations and the fibre is
  not, so `B` is not a function of the base and there is no skew product.
  Recorded here as well as in section 3 because the next connector should not
  re-run it: the settled data is *universal*, so any statistic of it is
  universal, so it cannot separate two configurations whose centre columns
  differ — and that is a two-line argument, not a measurement.
- **The centre column as a Toeplitz sequence.** Would have handed over an
  odometer factor and Downarowicz's whole toolbox. `0/2000` positions, to depth
  200,000. Seam: the array `(t, depth)` is Toeplitz and the centre column is
  its diagonal, and a diagonal is not a point.
- **Identifying the three-state automaton in the published classification.** I
  have `E` as an explicit invertible three-state Mealy automaton over two
  letters (`q0 = (q0,q2)`, `q1 = σ(q0,q2)`, `q2 = σ(q1,q2)`) and the
  classification of the 194 minimal such automata exists
  (<https://arxiv.org/abs/0803.3555>), but I could not fetch a table of the
  automata to match ours against, only the abstract. Left as a concrete,
  bounded task for whoever picks this up: identify the class, and ask whether
  the group is contracting — if it is, Nekrashevych's limit space is a genuinely
  new object attached to rule 30.
- **`E` as the odometer proper.** It is not: the order of `E` at level 14 is
  256 while the seed point's orbit is 64, so `E` is not level-transitive. This
  refines the death recorded in my first sighting (where I killed the odometer
  conjugacy at `m = 2` by a collision); the reason is now structural rather
  than a collision — `E` is a thin element, not a transitive one.
- **The accumulator `1/(1+D)` of stream-cipher design.** The right recurrence
  is literally one integrator over `GF(2)`, and the "output period doubles iff
  the input has odd weight per period" rule is that field's folklore. It buys
  the same single fact as the wreath product and stops at the same place: the
  input is an `OR`, so there is no transfer-function algebra past one division,
  and no linear-complexity argument applies. Kept as a row because it is a
  cheaper vocabulary for the same theorem if a theorist prefers it.
- **The wreath-product argument as a route past obstruction 7.** I thought for
  an hour that the tower's group theory would give the non-doubling half of
  `rightDiagonal_period_doubles_iff_odd_weight`. It does not, and the reason is
  exactly obstruction 7's: group theory bounds the **common** period of the
  first `k` diagonals and says nothing about whether an individual diagonal has
  a *shorter* period than its neighbours. What it does give is that the common
  period is `Q` or `2Q` and never anything else, which is section 5's topic 1
  and sidesteps the obstruction instead of overcoming it.
- **Anzai skew products as a single system.** The extension at depth `k` is an
  honest Anzai skew product, but the base is `Z/Q_k` and changes at every
  level, so the tower is a sequence of skew products, not one skew product with
  a cocycle to study. Every theorem in the Anzai literature I could reach is
  about a *fixed* base with an irrational rotation. Seam: our base is finite
  and grows.

## 5. What to hand the theorist

**Topic 1 (the one I would spend the session on). Restate the right-diagonal
doubling criterion about the *common* period, where it is provable, instead of
the *minimal* period, where obstruction 7 says it is not.** The board has
`rightDiagonal_antiperiodic_of_odd_driver` (the odd branch, including
`¬ PeriodicFrom L 0`) and treats the even branch as hard. The even branch is
hard only as a claim about minimality. As a claim about a period it is three
lines: by `rightDiagonal_recurrence`, `R_(k+2)(j + L) = R_(k+2)(j) XOR Σ_(i=1..L)
g(j+i)`, and `g` has period `L` because the two diagonals feeding it do, so
that sum is the same for every `j` and equals the weight parity. Hence

> `rightDiagonal_periodicFrom_step_of_even_driver (k L : ℕ)`
> `(hL0 : PeriodicFrom (rightDiagonal k) L 0)`
> `(hL1 : PeriodicFrom (rightDiagonal (k+1)) L 0)`
> `(heven : Even ((Finset.range L).sum (fun j => if rightDiagonal (k+1) (j+1) || rightDiagonal k (j+2) then 1 else 0)))`
> `: PeriodicFrom (rightDiagonal (k+2)) L 0`

This signature elaborates as written: `explorer/portage_scratch_evendriver.lean`,
`lake env lean`, only the `sorry` warning. It is the exact mirror of the odd lemma, sharpening `rightDiagonal_periodicFrom_step`
from `2 * L` to `L`. With it, the common period `Q_k` of all diagonals to depth
`k` is a power of two that doubles exactly at the odd-weight levels and is
otherwise unchanged, and *that* is the object the tower actually runs on: it is
the orbit period of the right-edge automorphism at level `k` (dictionary row 10
of 3.1, measured to level 15 by two independent implementations that agree
exactly). The depth that would settle it: none — it is a proof, not a
measurement, and the supporting identities fail 0 times on 39 levels. The one
thing to check first, because it would make the topic pointless: whether the
board already wants `Q` and I have missed it; I searched `Rule30/Statements.lean`
and found only the `2 * q` version.

**Topic 2. The coboundary equation as the wall's weakest sufficient
condition.** Put `centerColumn_other_of_cohomologous_column` (3.2) on the
board — it is a few lines — and then ask a theorist to attack, or to record as
an obstruction, the unconditional companion: *is there any `x ≠ 0` and `j` for
which `t ↦ centerColumn t XOR evolve (t + j) x` is eventually periodic?* It
depends on exactly one dictionary row: that a difference of two fibres is the
natural cohomological object, where "a column repeats" is not. The depth that
would settle it in the negative direction is already run — 1,616 pairs, no
period `≤ 4096` surviving from `t = 20,000` to `60,000`, longest partial run 17
steps — so what a theorist can add is either an obstruction (a reason no
difference can be eventually periodic, which would be a real theorem and might
follow from Kopra's width-2 result) or the observation that the free companion
`centerColumn_other_of_rightDiagonal_period_bounded` (3.3) closes the
bounded-period branch and so licenses assuming the periods grow.

## 6. Next vantage

**Algebraic and expansive subdynamics of `Z^2` actions** — Boyle–Lind
directional expansiveness, Kitchens–Schmidt, Ledrappier-type `Z^2` subshifts.
I named it last time as the vantage I could not reach, and this session has
made the case for it sharper rather than weaker: the reason every object in
this document fails is that the centre column is read at a depth that grows
with time, which is precisely the statement that the vertical direction is not
one of the directions in which this `Z^2` array is expansive or periodic, while
the two diagonal directions are. Directional expansiveness is the theory built
to say which directions in a space-time diagram carry the information, and the
picture hands it three measured slopes nobody has related — the seam at
`0.25 t`, the damage front at `0.24 t`, and the period exponent `2^(0.41 k)` —
in a setting where one diagonal direction is exactly periodic with no
transient and the other is eventually periodic. A connector coming from there
should be handed the identity `centerColumn t = e(t)_t` from 3.1 and asked
whether "the diagonal of a Toeplitz array" has a name in that field.

The vantage I could not reach from where I stood is **contracting self-similar
groups and Nekrashevych limit spaces**. I have the three-state automaton
explicitly and I could not determine whether the group it generates is
contracting, which is the gate to everything in that theory: a nucleus, a limit
space, an iterated monodromy interpretation. That is a bounded, concrete
computation — build the nucleus of `⟨q0, q1, q2⟩` and see whether it is finite
— and it needs somebody who knows the machinery rather than somebody who has
just met it. If the group is contracting, rule 30's right edge acquires a
compact limit space that no one has looked at, and the question of what the
diagonal `t ↦ (E^t δ)_t` means on it is the first thing to ask there.

I found search results related to the Boyle and Lind work on expansive subdynamics. Here's what the search revealed:

Boyle and Lind published a paper that provides a framework for studying the dynamics of commuting homeomorphisms, introducing a notion of expansiveness for continuous actions of ℤ^d on infinite compact metric spaces along subspaces of ℝ^d, and showing that there are nonexpansive subspaces in every dimension ≤ d-1.

The set of expansive k-dimensional subspaces is open in the Grassmann manifold of all k-dimensional subspaces of ℝ^d, and various dynamical properties are constant or vary nicely within a connected component of this set.

The seminal work is "Expansive subdynamics" by M. Boyle and D. Lind, published in Transactions of the American Mathematical Society, volume 349 (1997), pages 55-102.

This framework has been influential and has led to subsequent research. For instance, a later result showed that any direction in the plane occurs as the unique non-expansive direction of a ℤ² action, answering a question of Boyle and Lind.

## The Ledrappier Three-Dot System

The Ledrappier subshift is also known as the 3-dot system, and it is defined by f = 1 + x₁ + x₂ over F₂, where elements are the space-time diagrams of the binary state XOR cellular automaton.

## Algebraic Subshifts and Polynomial Factors

The Ledrappier subshift (the 3-dot system) and all two-dimensional algebraic subshifts over F_p defined by a polynomial without line polynomial factors in more than one direction have the property that every low complexity configuration is periodic.

## Non-expansive Directions

Research on Z² actions addresses non-expansive directions directly. One method involves translating the combinatorial problem to a question about the nonexpansive subspaces of a certain Z^d dynamical system. Additionally, for every direction ℓ in the plane there exists an expansive Z² action whose unique non-expansive direction is ℓ, and a set of directions occurs as the set of non-expansive directions for an expansive Z² action if and only if it is closed and non-empty.

The search results include academic papers on Nivat's conjecture, algebraic actions, and the structure of multi-dimensional symbolic dynamics systems, which are all central to understanding the Ledrappier example in this context.

Based on the web search results, I found information related to Sablik's work on directional dynamics in cellular automata:

The central idea of directional dynamics is to study the dynamical behavior of a cellular automaton through the conjoint action of its global rule (temporal action) and the shift map (spacial action): qualitative behaviors inherited from topological dynamics (equicontinuity, sensitivity, expansivity) are thus considered along arbitrary curves in space-time.

The formalism of directional dynamics was proposed by M. Sablik, with the key idea being to consider the action of the rule and that of the shift simultaneously.

In Sablik's work, each qualitative behavior of Kůrka's classification (equicontinuity, sensitivity, expansivity) is considered for different linear correlations between the two components, corresponding to different linear directions in space-time.

Regarding expansivity and directions: There exist one-dimensional positively pre-expansive cellular automata which are not positively expansive and they can be chosen reversible (while positive expansivity is impossible for reversible cellular automata).

The search results contain academic papers on this topic, but they don't contain specific information about "left-permutive theorem" in connection with directional dynamics. The results focus on the foundational concepts of directional dynamics and expansivity in cellular automata as developed by Sablik and his collaborators.

## Expansive and Nonexpansive Subspaces

**Expansiveness (from Boyle-Lind framework):**
"a ℤ^d-action by continuous maps (T^n: n∈ℤ^d) on a compact metric space X is expansive if there exists δ>0 such that for any distinct points x,y∈X, there exists n∈ℤ^d such that d(T^n x, T^n y)≥δ"

**Nonexpansiveness:**
A subspace V⊆ℝ^d is nonexpansive if it fails to satisfy the expansiveness condition; that is, "any subspace that is not expansive is called a nonexpansive subspace."

## Critical Results on Finiteness and Periodicity

**Theorem 1.3 (Boyle-Lind):** "For each 0≤k<d, there exists a k-dimensional subspace of ℝ^d that is nonexpansive."

**Key statement on double periodicity (from discussion following Theorem 1.3):**
"η is doubly periodic if and only if every subspace of ℝ^2 is expansive" (meaning no nonexpansive 1-dimensional subspaces exist).

## Key Findings

Guillon and Zinoviadis characterized the sets of non-expansive directions of subshifts of finite type (SFTs) in an unpublished manuscript, which also contains several realization results of SFTs with a unique non-expansive direction.

Using a deterministic version of the self-similar (hierarchical, or fixed-point) method for constructing 2-dimensional subshifts of finite type (SFTs), they construct aperiodic 2D SFTs with a unique direction of non-expansiveness and prove that the emptiness problem of SFTs is undecidable even in this restricted case.

As an additional application of their method, they characterize the sets of directions that can be the set of non-expansive directions of 2D SFTs.

Furthermore, a direction d is an expansive direction for a two-dimensional subshift if and only if both of the directions orthogonal to d are deterministic. This establishes the fundamental connection between deterministic directions and expansiveness that appears central to this line of research.

Guillon, Kari and Zinoviadis proved that the vertical and horizontal direction must indeed be non-expansive unless the associated SFT is vertically or horizontally periodic in the context of 4-way deterministic tile sets.

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about the Shereshevsky-Tisseur work on Lyapunov exponents and entropy in cellular automata:

The first definition of Lyapunov exponents (depending on a probability measure) for a one-dimensional cellular automaton were introduced by Shereshevsky in 1991. The existence of an almost everywhere constant value for each of the two exponents (left and right), requires particular conditions for the measure.

Shereshevsky establishes an inequality involving these two constants and the metric entropies of both the shift and the cellular automaton. Tisseur proved that the two Shereshevsky's exponents exist for a more suitable class of measures, then defined new exponents, called average Lyapunov exponents smaller or equal to the first ones. Two inequalities were obtained: the first one is analogous to the Shereshevsky's but concerns the average exponents; the second is the Shereshevsky inequality but with more suitable assumptions.

Shereshevsky establishes a first relation between the entropy of the shift and the entropy of the cellular automaton using some discrete analog of Lyapunov exponents for a CA ergodic measure, where the product of the shift entropy by the lyapunov exponents give an upper bound of the CA.

## 1. The problem, seen from outside

Take the map on bi-infinite rows of bits sending `b` to `b'` with
`b'(i) = b(i-1) XOR (b(i) OR b(i+1))`, and iterate it from the row that is `1`
at one place and `0` everywhere else. What grows is a triangle of bits, one row
per step, widening by one cell on each side. Write `c(t)` for the bit at the
origin after `t` steps. Known (Jen 1990): no two distinct vertical lines of this
triangle can both be eventually periodic. Known: `c` passes every statistical
test anyone has run, to great depth. Not known: whether `c` is eventually
periodic. The statement in front of me is the implication — **if `c` repeats,
some other vertical line repeats too** — which with Jen's result says `c` never
repeats, the first of Wolfram's prize questions. Nobody has a route.

**Restated in this vantage's own terms.** The set `X` of all bi-infinite
space-time diagrams of that map — all `y` in `{0,1}^(Z^2)` with
`y(t+1,x) = y(t,x-1) XOR (y(t,x) OR y(t,x+1))` for every `(t,x)` — is a
nearest-neighbour shift of finite type on `Z^2`, and the two coordinate shifts
generate a `Z^2` action on it. Boyle–Lind's expansive subdynamics asks, for each
line direction in `R^2`, whether a thickened band around a line in that
direction determines the whole diagram; the set `N(X)` of directions where it
does not is a closed, non-empty invariant of the system. The triangle is one
point `η` of `X` (one of its bi-infinite histories; the map is surjective, so
they exist), and the residual is a question about the *vertical* line direction
at one particular place: `c` is `η` read along the line `x = 0`, and the wall
says that if that read is eventually periodic then the read along some other
vertical line is too. In the linear members of this family — the Ledrappier
three-dot system and its relatives, where the defining relation is a polynomial
over `F_2` and the whole Kitchens–Schmidt apparatus applies — `N(X)` is the
finite set of edge directions of that polynomial's Newton polygon, and the
question can be answered by hand. Rule 30's relation is that of rule 150 plus
one quadratic monomial, `N(X)` swells from three directions to a closed arc, and
the vertical direction is in its interior.

## 3. Connections

### 3.1 The nonexpansive set of rule 30's space-time subshift is exactly the closed arc of velocities `v ≥ -1`, and the wall lives in its interior

**The claim.** The whole of Boyle–Lind's basic invariant is computable here by
hand, and I computed it: a band of velocity `v` (cells of space per row of time)
extends its determined region leftward at exactly `|1 - v|` cells per row and
rightward at exactly `max(0, -1 - v)` cells per row. So the expansive directions
of rule 30's space-time SFT are exactly the velocities `v < -1` — bands moving
left *faster than light* — and every other direction, including the vertical one
the wall is about, is nonexpansive. For the linear relatives the same arithmetic
gives three isolated nonexpansive directions, which are the edge directions of
the defining polynomial's Newton polygon.

**Seams.** (i) The whole expansive half of the theory is unreachable, because
the only expansive directions are steeper than the left light cone, and a
vertical line meets such a band once: `c(t)` is never a function of an expansive
subaction's state. This is the `Z^2` restatement of Portage's "the observable is
at depth `t`", and it is the same wall in different coordinates. (ii) My reach
rates are computed with the *uniform* deductions, valid for every diagram; a
particular diagram may be determined further by value-dependent steps, and the
measurement says how much further: switching on the rightward rule where the
pivot cell is white extends a vertical band's reach from `3` cells to `6` — **all
the free-bit structure in the picture buys exactly three columns**, because the
chain dies at the first black pivot. (iii) `N(X)` is an invariant of the
subshift, not of the point `η`; the orbit closure of the picture is a much
smaller system and I did not compute its `N`, which is a real gap.

**What it leans on.**

- The definition of an expansive line, fetched at
  <https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/0906.0609> (Hochman, *Non-expansive
  directions for `Z^2` actions*): *"Then ℓ is said to be an expansive line if
  there exist r>0 and δ>0 such that, for all x,y∈X, d(T^u x,T^u y)<δ for all
  u∈ℓ^r∩ℤ² ⟹ x=y"*, and *"Expansiveness only depends on the direction of the
  line and not the line itself, so we may speak of expansive and non-expansive
  directions."*
- Boyle–Lind's basic fact, from the same page: *"It was shown that this set is
  closed and, when the phase space is infinite, non-empty; and furthermore if C
  is any closed set of directions of cardinality |C|≥2, then it is the set of
  non-expansive directions for some action."* And in the same words at
  <https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1603.05464> (Zinoviadis), Proposition 9:
  *"𝒩(X) is closed. In addition, 𝒩(X) is empty if and only if X is finite."*
- Sablik's theorem in the held text
  `sources/kurka-topological-dynamics-1d-ca.txt`, Theorem 32 (lines 611–614):
  *"(1) If F is left-permutive, then X− (F ) = ( −∞ , −m). (2) If F is
  right-permutive, then X+(F ) = ( −a, ∞ )."* Rule 30 has memory `m = -1`, so
  `X^-(F) = (-∞, 1)`; it is not right-permutive and (Theorem 33) not

### 3.2 Rule 30 is rule 150 plus one quadratic monomial, and the residual is **false** for rule 150 and for rule 90

**The claim.** Over `F_2`, `a OR b = a + b + ab`, so rule 30's local rule is

```
    l XOR (c OR r)  =  l + c + r + c·r  =  rule 150  +  c·r
```

— rule 150 with one quadratic monomial added, flipping exactly two of the eight
table entries (`150 XOR (2^3 + 2^7) = 30`). Rule 150's space-time diagrams are an
*algebraic* `Z^2` subshift in the sense of the Ledrappier world, annihilated by
`XY + 1 + X + X^2` over `F_2`; rule 90's by `XY + 1 + X^2`; Ledrappier's own
three-dot system is the two-cell XOR automaton, rule 102. In that whole linear
family the columns question is answerable, and **the answer is the opposite of
the one the residual wants**: rule 150's centre column is identically black
while its column 1 is provably not eventually periodic, and rule 90's centre
column is white from time 1 on while no other column near it is eventually
periodic. Each of them has *exactly one* eventually periodic column. So each of
them satisfies Jen's conclusion — no two columns both repeat — and falsifies the
residual. Any proof of this wall must therefore use the monomial `c·r`, and no
argument available to rule 90 or rule 150 can be the proof.

**The dictionary.**

### 3.3 The residual is the missing half of a deterministic direction, and the field names it

**The claim.** In the `Z^2` vocabulary, a direction is expansive exactly when
both half-planes bounded by it are *deterministic*. Rule 30's vertical direction
is deterministic on one side and not on the other, and everything the project
knows about the columns is the deterministic side while everything it needs is
the other. Jen's sandwich lemma and Kopra's width-2 theorem are, in this
language, statements about the deterministic half-plane; the residual is the
first statement that needs the non-deterministic one, and that is exactly why
nothing on the board reaches it.

### 3.5 The picture's block complexity, and why no Nivat-type theorem can reach the wall — including "the diagonal of a Toeplitz array"

**The claim.** The Nivat/Cyr–Kra machinery is the only part of `Z^2` symbolic
dynamics that is about an individual configuration rather than a subshift, which
makes it the natural home for a question about one picture. It cannot reach this
wall, and the measurement says by how far: the picture's complexity exceeds
Nivat's threshold by a factor of `364` already at `(w,h) = (2,8)`, and — the part
worth recording — **even the settled region, which is built entirely out of
periodic words, has exponential block complexity**, because the periods are
unbounded. The same measurement answers the brief's other question: the right-edge
array is periodic in time at every fixed depth, but its period subgroup at a cell
has infinite index in `Z^2`, so it is not a Toeplitz array in this field's sense,
and a diagonal read of it has no name here because there is no subaction to take.

**The dictionary.**

| Nivat's hypothesis | `P(w,h) ≤ wh` for some `w,h` | — |
| Cyr–Kra's theorem | `P(n,k) ≤ nk/2` for some `n,k` implies `η` is periodic | quoted below |
| The picture's complexity in the transient band | `P(2,8) = 2916`, `P(4,8) = 11663`, `P(1,16) = 65536` (all `2^16` column words occur) | measured, rows 2,000–3,980 |
| The picture's complexity in the settled region | `P(2,8) = 2778`, `P(1,16) = 21005` — smaller, still exponential | measured |
| The picture's complexity on the right | `P(2,8) = 2916` — indistinguishable from the band | measured |
| The complexity of the whole space-time SFT | Exactly `2^(w + 2(h-1))` blocks satisfy the rule internally | arithmetic: `wh - (h-1)(w-2)` free cells |
| So the `Z^2` entropy of `X` | Zero — the entropy is one-dimensional: **entropy rank one** | same arithmetic |
| "`η` doubly periodic" | "every direction is expansive" | quoted below |
| "some column of `η` is eventually periodic" | **No translation.** It is periodicity of a *restriction to one line*, not a period vector | this is the seam |

## 1. The problem, seen from outside

Take the map on bi-infinite rows of bits sending `b` to `b'` with
`b'(i) = b(i-1) XOR (b(i) OR b(i+1))`, and iterate it from the row that is `1`
at one place and `0` everywhere else. What grows is a triangle of bits, one row
per step, widening by one cell on each side. Write `c(t)` for the bit at the
origin after `t` steps. Known (Jen 1990): no two distinct vertical lines of this
triangle can both be eventually periodic. Known: `c` passes every statistical
test anyone has run, to great depth. Not known: whether `c` is eventually
periodic. The statement in front of me is the implication — **if `c` repeats,
some other vertical line repeats too** — which with Jen's result says `c` never
repeats, the first of Wolfram's prize questions. Nobody has a route.

**Restated in this vantage's own terms.** The set `X` of all bi-infinite
space-time diagrams of that map — all `y` in `{0,1}^(Z^2)` with
`y(t+1,x) = y(t,x-1) XOR (y(t,x) OR y(t,x+1))` for every `(t,x)` — is a
nearest-neighbour shift of finite type on `Z^2`, and the two coordinate shifts
generate a `Z^2` action on it. Boyle–Lind's expansive subdynamics asks, for each
line direction in `R^2`, whether a thickened band around a line in that
direction determines the whole diagram; the set `N(X)` of directions where it
does not is a closed, non-empty invariant of the system. The triangle is one
point `η` of `X` (one of its bi-infinite histories; the map is surjective, so
they exist), and the residual is a question about the *vertical* line direction
at one particular place: `c` is `η` read along the line `x = 0`, and the wall
says that if that read is eventually periodic then the read along some other
vertical line is too. In the linear members of this family — the Ledrappier
three-dot system and its relatives, where the defining relation is a polynomial
over `F_2` and the whole Kitchens–Schmidt apparatus applies — `N(X)` is the
finite set of edge directions of that polynomial's Newton polygon, and the
question can be answered by hand. Rule 30's relation is that of rule 150 plus
one quadratic monomial, `N(X)` swells from three directions to a closed arc, and
the vertical direction is in its interior.

## 3. Connections

### 3.1 The nonexpansive set of rule 30's space-time subshift is exactly the closed arc of velocities `v ≥ -1`, and the wall lives in its interior

**The claim.** The whole of Boyle–Lind's basic invariant is computable here by
hand, and I computed it: a band of velocity `v` (cells of space per row of time)
extends its determined region leftward at exactly `|1 - v|` cells per row and
rightward at exactly `max(0, -1 - v)` cells per row. So the expansive directions
of rule 30's space-time SFT are exactly the velocities `v < -1` — bands moving
left *faster than light* — and every other direction, including the vertical one
the wall is about, is nonexpansive. For the linear relatives the same arithmetic
gives three isolated nonexpansive directions, which are the edge directions of
the defining polynomial's Newton polygon.

**Seams.** (i) The whole expansive half of the theory is unreachable, because
the only expansive directions are steeper than the left light cone, and a
vertical line meets such a band once: `c(t)` is never a function of an expansive
subaction's state. This is the `Z^2` restatement of Portage's "the observable is
at depth `t`", and it is the same wall in different coordinates. (ii) My reach
rates are computed with the *uniform* deductions, valid for every diagram; a
particular diagram may be determined further by value-dependent steps, and the
measurement says how much further: switching on the rightward rule where the
pivot cell is white extends a vertical band's reach from `3` cells to `6` — **all
the free-bit structure in the picture buys exactly three columns**, because the
chain dies at the first black pivot. (iii) `N(X)` is an invariant of the
subshift, not of the point `η`; the orbit closure of the picture is a much
smaller system and I did not compute its `N`, which is a real gap.

identical closure for rule 90 with its three uniform deductions and reproduces

(rightward) and `v = +1` (leftward). That control is the reason to believe the
rule 30 numbers. To falsify: exhibit a fourth uniform deduction for rule 30, or a
`v ≥ -1` and a band half-width from which the rightward reach is unbounded.

project's tools work — the diagonals, the seam, `leftSolve` — is a direction in
which the picture is determined leftward, and the wall is the one place where
rightward determination is needed and the rate is exactly zero. What remains is

### 3.2 Rule 30 is rule 150 plus one quadratic monomial, and the residual is **false** for rule 150 and for rule 90

**The claim.** Over `F_2`, `a OR b = a + b + ab`, so rule 30's local rule is

```
    l XOR (c OR r)  =  l + c + r + c·r  =  rule 150  +  c·r
```

— rule 150 with one quadratic monomial added, flipping exactly two of the eight
table entries (`150 XOR (2^3 + 2^7) = 30`). Rule 150's space-time diagrams are an
*algebraic* `Z^2` subshift in the sense of the Ledrappier world, annihilated by
`XY + 1 + X + X^2` over `F_2`; rule 90's by `XY + 1 + X^2`; Ledrappier's own
three-dot system is the two-cell XOR automaton, rule 102. In that whole linear
family the columns question is answerable, and **the answer is the opposite of
the one the residual wants**: rule 150's centre column is identically black
while its column 1 is provably not eventually periodic, and rule 90's centre
column is white from time 1 on while no other column near it is eventually
periodic. Each of them has *exactly one* eventually periodic column. So each of
them satisfies Jen's conclusion — no two columns both repeat — and falsifies the
residual. Any proof of this wall must therefore use the monomial `c·r`, and no
argument available to rule 90 or rule 150 can be the proof.

**The dictionary.**

### 3.3 The residual is the missing half of a deterministic direction, and the field names it

**The claim.** In the `Z^2` vocabulary, a direction is expansive exactly when
both half-planes bounded by it are *deterministic*. Rule 30's vertical direction
is deterministic on one side and not on the other, and everything the project
knows about the columns is the deterministic side while everything it needs is
the other. Jen's sandwich lemma and Kopra's width-2 theorem are, in this
language, statements about the deterministic half-plane; the residual is the
first statement that needs the non-deterministic one, and that is exactly why
nothing on the board reaches it.

### 3.5 The picture's block complexity, and why no Nivat-type theorem can reach the wall — including "the diagonal of a Toeplitz array"

**The claim.** The Nivat/Cyr–Kra machinery is the only part of `Z^2` symbolic
dynamics that is about an individual configuration rather than a subshift, which
makes it the natural home for a question about one picture. It cannot reach this
wall, and the measurement says by how far: the picture's complexity exceeds
Nivat's threshold by a factor of `364` already at `(w,h) = (2,8)`, and — the part
worth recording — **even the settled region, which is built entirely out of
periodic words, has exponential block complexity**, because the periods are
unbounded. The same measurement answers the brief's other question: the right-edge
array is periodic in time at every fixed depth, but its period subgroup at a cell
has infinite index in `Z^2`, so it is not a Toeplitz array in this field's sense,
and a diagonal read of it has no name here because there is no subaction to take.

**The dictionary.**

| Cyr–Kra's theorem | `P(n,k) ≤ nk/2` for some `n,k` implies `η` is periodic | quoted below |
| The picture's complexity in the transient band | `P(2,8) = 2916`, `P(4,8) = 11663`, `P(1,16) = 65536` (all `2^16` column words occur) | measured, rows 2,000–3,980 |

| "`η` doubly periodic" | "every direction is expansive" | quoted below |

## 4. Died in translation

- **The vertical direction as an expansive direction of the orbit closure.** My
  first hope: if the vertical direction were expansive for the orbit closure of
  the picture (a much smaller system than the full SFT), then a point whose
  vertical band is periodic would be globally periodic and every column would
  repeat. It dies twice. Structurally: expansiveness of the vertical direction
  gives Jen's sandwich lemma, not the residual — it upgrades *all* columns in a
  band being periodic, and we are given *one*. Empirically: rule 90 has the
  vertical direction expansive with constant 1 and the residual fails for it.
  Seam: expansiveness is a statement about a band, and the hypothesis is about a
  line.
- **Kitchens–Schmidt rigidity for the settled region.** The settled region is
  built from words of period `2^k` and looked like a candidate algebraic
  subshift, where the dual-module machinery would apply. It is not: the settled
  configuration is itself a rule 30 evolution (crystal 47), so it satisfies the
  quadratic relation, not a linear one, and there is no group. Seam: the same
  `OR` that kills 3.2 kills this, and obstruction 4 already says the settled
  region carries no information about the boundary anyway.
- **The amoeba / Newton polygon of the defining relation.** For a linear rule the
  nonexpansive directions are the edge directions of the Newton polygon, which I
  verified for rule 90 by an independent method. For rule 30 the "polygon" of
  `l + c + r + c·r` would have to carry a degree-2 vertex, and the object with a
  Newton polygon is a polynomial ideal that does not exist here. Seam: `N(X_30)`
  is an arc, and an arc is not a set of edge directions of any polygon.
- **Milnor directional entropy as the bridge between the slopes.** `h_α` is
  convex and continuous *on the expansive directions* (Boyle–Lind, Theorem 59 in
  the held Kůrka notes). Rule 30's expansive directions are `v < -1`, a region
  outside the light cone where the entropy is `|m+α|·ln|A|` by Proposition 58(5)
  and the picture is white. So the convexity theorem covers exactly the part of
  the direction circle where nothing happens. Seam: the theory's regularity

## 5. What to hand the theorist

**Topic 1 (the one I would spend the session on). The linear no-go: make it a
standing test that every candidate lemma must pass.** The claim to falsify is the
one in 3.2:

> Rule 150 from a single black cell has a second eventually periodic column —
> some `x ≠ 0` and `p > 0` with `cell(t + p, x) = cell(t, x)` for all large `t`.

It depends on exactly one dictionary row: that rule 30's local rule is rule 150
plus the monomial `c·r`, which is arithmetic (`150 XOR 136 = 30`). The evidence
against it is that rule 150's centre column is *identically black* — provable in
two lines from `P_t = (1+u+u^2)^t` and Frobenius, and measured `10^7/10^7` — while
its column 1 obeys `a(2t) = 0`, `a(2t+1) = 1 XOR a(t)`, from which eventual
periodicity fails by a three-line descent (an odd period forces `a ≡ 1` on a tail,
contradicting `a(2t)=0`; an even period `2p'` makes `p'` a period too). Both
identities are checked with 0 failures on `2·10^6` rows, and the density `1/3`
they force is measured as `0.333334`. The depth that would settle it: none needed
in the negative direction — it is a proof — and `|x| ≤ 64` at `p ≤ 4096` over
20,000 rows in the positive direction. **What to do with it is the point.** It
gives the board a ten-minute falsifier for every proposed route to this wall: run
the same argument on rule 150. Surjectivity, left-permutivity, the light cone,
the space-time SFT, entropy rank one, the sandwich lemma, and expansiveness of the
vertical direction all survive that test and therefore cannot be the proof — and
rule 90, which has *more* structure than rule 30 in every one of those respects,
is the witness. The one thing to check first, because it would kill the topic:
whether some column of rule 150 or rule 90 beyond `|x| = 64` is eventually
periodic. For rule 150 that is implausible — the columns are dense, so the sparse
artefact that fooled my first script cannot hide there — but it is unproved.

**Topic 2. State the seam bound in the language that names it, and see whether the
name is load-bearing.** The claim, from 3.4's dictionary, is that these are the
same statement:

> `leftDiagonal_onset_le` (onset `≤ k` for every diagonal)
> `⟺` the seam never runs faster than half a cell per row
> `⟺` the left Lyapunov exponent of rule 30 at the seed satisfies `λ^- ≤ 1/2`.

The first two are obstruction 6's equivalence; the third is the field's name for
the same quantity, and the conversion between the diagonal parametrisation and
the picture parametrisation is exactly `α ↦ α/(1+α)`, which sends the measured
onset `0.336` to `0.2515` against a measured seam of `0.2497`. It depends on one
dictionary row: that the damage front the obstruction is about *is* `λ^-`. What
a theorist can add: whether anything in the Lyapunov-exponent literature bounds
`λ^-` above for a *specific* configuration rather than almost everywhere. My
reading says no — Shereshevsky's inequality and Bressaud–Tisseur's theorem both
bound the exponents *below* — and if that reading is right the honest outcome is
a new obstruction entry saying so, which is worth having, because three separate
board items (`leftDiagonal_onset_le`, obstruction 3's horizon, `crystals` A3) are
the same unproved bound wearing three names.
